full_text_en:
China Wuhan Changjiang Shipping Company Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation v. Soto Grande Shipping Corp., S.A., Panama — dispute over crew employment contract

Plaintiff: China Wuhan Changjiang Shipping Company Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation

Legal Representative: Zhang Jishan, Manager of China Wuhan Changjiang Shipping Company Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation

Agent ad litem: Zhuang Yinsen, lawyer at Shanghai Maritime Law Firm

Agent ad litem: Ni Zhiqiang, lawyer at Shanghai Maritime Law Firm

Defendant: Soto Grande Shipping Corp., S.A., Panama

Legal Representative: Alan A. McCarthy, Director/President of Soto Grande Shipping Corp., S.A., Panama

The plaintiff, China Wuhan Changjiang Shipping Company Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation, filed an action with the Shanghai Maritime Court against the defendant, Soto Grande Shipping Corp., S.A., Panama, regarding a dispute over a crew employment contract.

The crew employment contract signed by the plaintiff and the defendant specified that the plaintiff would dispatch 25 crew members, including the captain, to work on board the Panamanian-flagged vessel "M.V. Pomona," owned by the defendant, for a period of one year. During the period of employment, the defendant was to remit $20,833 in crew wages to the plaintiff's account on the 5th of each month. The plaintiff began performing the contract on January 14, 1985. However, by September 16, 1985, the defendant had only paid a small amount of expenses and had failed to remit the full wages as stipulated in the contract, with arrears totaling $225,283.05, thereby affecting the livelihood of the 25 crew members and their families. Consequently, on September 16, 1985, the plaintiff filed an application with the Shanghai Maritime Court for the arrest of the "M.V. Pomona," seeking an order that the defendant provide security of $200,000, up to the sale of the vessel to satisfy its debts. Upon review, the Shanghai Maritime Court found that the plaintiff's application met the conditions for arresting a ship and had a reasonable basis, and on September 28 of the same year, it ordered the arrest of the vessel.

On October 3, 1985, the plaintiff filed a claim with the Shanghai Maritime Court, seeking, in addition to the aforementioned arrears in crew wages, the costs of fuel supplied to the vessel, the application fee for ship arrest, legal fees, liquidated damages, and interest on the related expenses, totaling $259,636.03.

As the defendant did not provide security, in order to protect the lawful rights and interests of the parties, the Shanghai Maritime Court, in accordance with Article 93(3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), which provides that "the people's court may sell items that are seized or impounded and are not suitable for long-term storage, and retain the proceeds," ordered the sale of the "M.V. Pomona."

On October 18, 1985, the "M.V. Pomona" was sold by public auction, and the proceeds of $430,000 were preserved. At the same time, the Shanghai Maritime Court announced that all creditors of the vessel should register their claims within 30 days.

The defendant did not file a responsive pleading within the statutory period. After being properly summoned twice by the Shanghai Maritime Court, the defendant failed to appear in court without any justifiable reason. Accordingly, the case was tried on February 25, 1987.

Upon trial, the Shanghai Maritime Court found the following facts: On December 17, 1984, the plaintiff and the defendant signed a crew employment contract in Shanghai. On January 14, 1985, the plaintiff dispatched 25 crew members to board the "M.V. Pomona" in accordance with the contract, thereby commencing performance of the contract. During their employment, the crew members accepted the defendant's assignments and directions, performed their respective duties as stipulated in the contract, and provided labor services to the defendant. The defendant raised no objections to the labor services provided by the plaintiff. During this period, the plaintiff received only two remittances from the defendant, totaling $21,455, on February 1 and June 12 of the same year. Additionally, on August 21 and September 22, 1985, the defendant provided $840.8 for the crew's meals.

In early October 1985, to meet the daily needs of the vessel during its detention, the plaintiff supplied 16 tons of #0 light diesel oil to the vessel, which, including lighterage costs, amounted to $3,500.

Article 4 of the crew employment contract entered into between the plaintiff and the defendant provided that the shipowner should pay the plaintiff $20,833 in service fees on a monthly basis. The defendant unilaterally breached the contract, and by the time the plaintiff filed the lawsuit, the defendant had been in arrears for nine months, totaling $190,149.24.

The Shanghai Maritime Court held that the service contract entered into between the plaintiff and the defendant was in conformity with the laws of China and that both parties should perform it in good faith. The plaintiff and the crew members it dispatched had continuously and diligently performed the contract until the "M.V. Pomona" was compulsorily sold by the court. The defendant's long-term failure to pay the substantial service fees affected the normal lives of the crew members and their families. In light of the defendant's serious breach of contract, the plaintiff's application for the arrest of the "M.V. Pomona," owned by the defendant, in order to exercise its maritime claim, was justified. As the owner of the "M.V. Pomona," the defendant, having long failed to pay the service fees, violated the contract and shall bear full responsibility for the consequences arising from its unfulfilled obligations. The plaintiff's supply of fuel oil to the vessel during the period of its arrest by the court should be considered an act taken to preserve the vessel for the common benefit of all creditors.

In accordance with Article 113 of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation) and with reference to international practice, the Shanghai Maritime Court rendered judgment on September 21, 1987, as follows:

1. The defendant shall pay the plaintiff $190,149.24 in earned service fees.

2. The defendant shall pay the plaintiff $3,500 in fuel supply costs.

3. The plaintiff's other claims are not supported.

4. The court acceptance fee of $1,176.87, the application fee for ship arrest of $625, and other litigation costs of $139.90, totaling $1,941.77, shall be borne by the defendant. After this judgment takes effect, these costs shall be deducted from the proceeds from the sale of the "M.V. Pomona."

The costs of $25,185.88 incurred for the compulsory sale of the "M.V. Pomona" and for the satisfaction of debts shall be deducted first from the proceeds of the sale of the vessel.

The execution of Item 1 above shall, after this judgment takes effect, be satisfied jointly by the plaintiff and other creditors of the "M.V. Pomona" from the proceeds of the sale of the vessel. The execution of Item 2 above shall, after this judgment takes effect, be paid from the proceeds of the sale.

After the judgment was served, neither the plaintiff nor the defendant appealed. The judgment became effective. The Shanghai Maritime Court, in accordance with the Supreme People's Court's Specific Provisions on Compulsory Sale of Arrested Ships to Satisfy Debts, on December 9 and 10, 1987, convened a creditors' meeting. By making public the distributable amount, the order of satisfaction, and the nature and amounts of each creditor's claims, and by allowing full consultation among the creditors, the debts in the "M.V. Pomona" case were satisfied. Upon examination of the creditor documents and the amounts of claims, four creditors and their claim amounts were confirmed as follows:

1. The claim of the Shanghai Maritime Administration Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation: crew wages totaling $171,840.26.

2. The claim of the China Ocean Shipping Agency, Ningbo Branch: port charges, supplies, and other expenses totaling $23,292.18.

3. The claim of the Shanghai Shipbuilding Industry Corporation Ship Repair Center: ship repair costs of $39,000.

4. The claim of the Westminster National Bank of the United States: a mortgage loan of $1,931,530.34.

The amount of $190,149.24 in service fees to be paid by the defendant to the plaintiff, as determined in the judgment of the Shanghai Maritime Court dated September 21, 1987, also participated in the satisfaction.

The proceeds from the sale of the "M.V. Pomona" amounted to $430,000. After deducting, in accordance with the law, the costs of the vessel sale and debt satisfaction, totaling $25,185.88, fuel costs during the arrest period of $3,500, and the application fee for ship arrest and litigation costs payable by the defendant of $1,941.77, the remaining amount was $399,372.35. Adding the interest on the proceeds from the vessel sale in the current deposit account at the Bank of China in the amount of $17,921.67, the actual amount available for distribution was $417,294.02.

According to the order of satisfaction prescribed in the Supreme People's Court's Specific Provisions on Compulsory Sale of Arrested Ships to Satisfy Debts, the claims included in the first priority of satisfaction were: the service fees of $190,149.24 due to the Wuhan Changjiang Shipping Company Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation and the crew service fees of $171,840.26 due to the Shanghai Maritime Administration Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation. Among the claims of the China Ocean Shipping Agency, Ningbo Branch, the amounts of $9,574.29, representing state taxes, port fees, and other port charges, could be included in the second priority of satisfaction. The mortgage loan of the Westminster National Bank of the United States, falling between the fourth and fifth priorities of satisfaction, could receive $45,730.23.

During the consultations, the ship repair costs of $39,000 claimed by the Shanghai Shipbuilding Industry Corporation Ship Repair Center and the water and oil supply costs of $13,717.89 claimed by the China Ocean Shipping Agency, Ningbo Branch, were classified as "other registered claims" in the fifth priority and would receive no satisfaction. These creditors argued that the incurrence of these claims had benefited the other creditors to some extent, yet they themselves would receive no or very little satisfaction. They requested that the creditors receiving more satisfaction appropriately compensate them for their losses. After further consultations, the Shanghai Maritime Administration Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation, taking into account the role played by the plaintiff in this case, agreed to assign $12,400.26 from its own recovery amount to the plaintiff. The Shanghai Maritime Administration and the Westminster National Bank of the United States, considering the actual losses of the Shanghai Shipbuilding Corporation and the Ningbo Branch, agreed to provide appropriate compensation from their recovery amounts. As a result, the five parties reached the following settlement agreement for satisfaction:

The Wuhan Changjiang Shipping Company Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation shall receive $202,549.50;

The Shanghai Maritime Administration Seafarers Foreign Technical Service Corporation shall receive $150,000;

The China Ocean Shipping Agency, Ningbo Branch shall receive $15,274.29;

The Westminster National Bank of the United States shall receive $44,970.23;

The Shanghai Shipbuilding Industry Corporation shall receive $4,500.

Upon review, the Shanghai Maritime Court found the settlement agreement to be lawful, fair, and voluntary, and confirmed it.
